narrative:
The model estimated a 54% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means failure was judged slightly more likely than passing, so your application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty; it still leaves a meaningful chance that you would pass.

The strongest reason was your LSAT score. At 25, it was well below the average of about 37 among accepted students, and it was the feature that pushed most strongly toward a predicted bar-exam failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23; this was the second most influential feature and it pushed in your favor, toward passing. Your third-year class standing, at the fourth decile, was the third most influential feature and also worked mildly in your favor, though not enough to offset the LSAT concern.

To improve a future application, focus first on the LSAT: use structured preparation, take practice tests, and consider retaking it if you can raise your score. Seek admissions advising about whether to reapply after a stronger LSAT, and ask whether a human review can consider any contextual factors. A higher LSAT would most directly reduce the failure risk the model identified.
